title: Easter Monday
hookLine: a day for walking, like Emmaus; in some places the Emmaus walk

cards: Two friends are walking out of Jerusalem, late in the day, toward a village called Emmaus. They're going over it all: the arrest, the cross, and that morning's strange report from some women of an empty tomb.
A stranger falls into step and asks what they're talking about. They stop, faces sad, and Cleopas more or less says: are you the only person around here who hasn't heard? He lets them tell it.
Then he starts to talk, and the road gets shorter. Some places keep the day after Easter just like this, with a walk. Today, Easter Monday.

teach.h: THAT SAME DAY, ON AN ORDINARY ROAD.
teach.b: Luke is careful about one detail: this happens on Easter day itself. So why does a Monday borrow it?
Because the morning after a great feast is when ordinary life starts again, and this is Easter turning up on an ordinary road.
In the King James Bible: "Jesus himself drew near, and went with them." But Luke says their eyes were held.
He walks the whole way as a stranger, going through Moses and the prophets, explaining the things written about himself.
At the village he makes as if to keep walking, and they press him: "Abide with us: for it is toward evening, and the day is far spent." So he comes in.
At the table he takes bread, blesses it, breaks it and hands it to them, and they know him. Then he's gone from their sight.

And they say to each other: "Did not our heart burn within us, while he talked with us by the way, and while he opened to us the scriptures?" They knew him at the table, but the burning started on the road.
Readers find layers here. Some hear an echo of communion in the breaking of bread. Some hear the risen Christ walking beside people who don't yet see him.
Others notice the plain hospitality: two tired travelers invite a stranger in at dusk. Then the last turn.

teach.h: KNOWN IN THE BREAKING OF BREAD.
teach.b: That same hour they hurry back to Jerusalem to tell the others how he was "known of them in breaking of bread."

how: In some places Christians keep Easter Monday with an Emmaus walk, going out together on foot after the feast, and some churches read Luke's Emmaus story in the days after Easter.

games.q: you're one of the two. you've reached your village at dusk, and the stranger makes as if to walk on. what do you do?
o: press him to stay: it's evening, and the day is far spent.
ask him to come back tomorrow.
games.why: they press him: "abide with us." he comes in, and at the table, as he breaks the bread, they know him.

practice: Bring to mind one person you could walk beside, not to fix anything, just to talk, and picture the route: a park, the long way to the shop.
Leave a gap in the talk you imagine, because the Emmaus story happens in the gap nobody planned. If you pray, ask that the road be good company; if you don't, just hold that person in mind.

wordCard.voice: Easter Monday. The day after Easter, kept in some places with a walk, remembering the road to Emmaus and the stranger who turned out to be the risen Jesus.

orig.note: Greek: bread, a loaf. Luke says he was known to them in the breaking of bread.
